extracted.intended_audience: general readers, fans, media students, and researchers interested in the television series Rick and Morty
extracted.subtask_description: An encyclopedic Wikipedia article describing the creation, production, themes, reception, and related media for the television series Rick and Morty. Covers writing methods, animation techniques, broadcast details, critical response, and franchise activity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of Harmon's story circle and two-act structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Many episodes are structured with use of a story circle, a Harmon creation based largely on Joseph Campbell's monomyth; its two-act structure places the act break at an odd location in the stages of the monomyth (after The Meeting with the Goddess, instead of Atonement with the Father).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Episodes typically follow this story-circle-backed two-act design when developing consistency and logical beginning, middle, and conclusion; writers break the story with this structure in mind to guide outlines and drafts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intended discontinuous storylines / lack of traditional continuity
rubrics_metrics.description: The creators have stated intentions for the series to lack traditional continuity, opting for discontinuous storylines 'not bound by rules'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Creative choice: episodes need not strictly adhere to serialized continuity; this enables stand-alone adventures and tonal flexibility but may require careful handling to avoid confusing audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of revisiting old tropes (minimize fan service)
rubrics_metrics.description: Writers avoid revisiting old tropes from the show's past 'in fear of that coming off as disingenuous fan service.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When producing new episodes, avoid gratuitous callbacks or recycling past tropes purely to please fans; favor genuine narrative or character-driven reasons for references.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collaborative iterative writing process with outlines and creator passes
rubrics_metrics.description: The writing staff first meets and discusses ideas that evolve into a story; after breaking the story a writer is assigned to create an outline. Roiland and Harmon do a 'pass' on the outline, and the episode undergoes several more drafts. The final draft of the script is last approved by either of the co-creators.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Production practice: use a small writers' room to brainstorm, break stories collaboratively, assign outlines, then iterate through passes by showrunners until final approval. Note: Harmon perfectionism has been cited as a cause of schedule delays.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improvisation in voice recording to enhance naturalness
rubrics_metrics.description: When recording dialogue, Roiland does a considerable amount of improvisation, in order to make the characters feel more natural.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allow voice actors room for improvisation during recording sessions to capture spontaneity and character authenticity; integrate useful improvised material into script drafts where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Animation pipeline and software choices
rubrics_metrics.description: Animation for the show is done using Toon Boom Harmony (a vector-based 2D puppet software); post-production work is done in Adobe After Effects, and background art is done in Adobe Photoshop.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Technical guideline: choose economical and efficient tools (Harmony for puppet-based 2D animation) and standard post/graphics tools (After Effects, Photoshop) to manage costs and workflow for episodic animation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Art/style guide: odd or asymmetrical character features
rubrics_metrics.description: Season three art director explained that the characters are often drawn with odd or asymmetrical features, in order to avoid looking 'too normal to live in the Rick and Morty universe.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Visual guideline: deliberately incorporate asymmetry and eccentric design elements in characters and backgrounds to sustain the show's distinctive surreal aesthetic (examples include small 'w-shaped mouths').

rubrics_metrics.name: Episode runtime and segment format
rubrics_metrics.description: The show runs approximately 22 minutes per episode; Roiland initially wanted one eleven-minute segment, but Adult Swim pushed for a half-hour program.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Format constraint: scripts and story structure should be planned for a ~22-minute runtime (half-hour broadcast slot), which affects pacing, act structure, and story scope. Short-segment formats (11 min) are an option but may be constrained by network preferences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Broadcast rating considerations (TV-14 / TV-MA)
rubrics_metrics.description: For the first season Adult Swim placed a tamer-than-usual TV-14 rating on the program; many later episodes have received TV-MA ratings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Content and scheduling: be aware of content ratings and how airtime and target audience may influence permissible language, violence, and adult themes. Ratings decisions can shape creative choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of metafictional and postmodern devices (fourth-wall acknowledgements)
rubrics_metrics.description: Occasionally, characters will acknowledge an episode's narrative or hint at the presence of a fourth wall, suggesting that they are aware of the fact that they are characters of a TV show.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Narrative device: apply self-reflexive/postmodern moments (meta jokes, fourth-wall nods) strategically to enhance humor and commentary; balance such devices with humanistic elements so the show remains emotionally resonant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comedic formula: juxtaposition of interdimensional hijinks and domestic family drama
rubrics_metrics.description: The general formula consists of the juxtaposition of an extremely selfish, alcoholic grandfather dragging his grandson along for interdimensional adventures, intercut with domestic family drama.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tone guideline: maintain a balance between high-concept sci-fi adventures and grounded family dynamics to create the show's signature mix of absurdity and emotional grounding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Flexible episode ordering to serve broader series logic
rubrics_metrics.description: In producing the series' first season, episodes were occasionally written out of order (e.g., 'Rick Potion #9' was the second episode written but animated as the fifth) because ordering better served series continuity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Production scheduling: be prepared to alter episode production or air order to improve narrative flow or continuity; ensure continuity/logistics are tracked if episodes move positions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Small, non-unionized writers' room staffing model (production characteristic)
rubrics_metrics.description: The series' early writing staff was 'very, very tiny' and, like many Adult Swim productions, was not unionized with the Writers Guild of America.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operational note: small, tightly collaborative writing teams can produce heavy output per writer, but staffing and labor practices (union status, petitions) can affect schedules, morale, and production negotiations.
